weeks.title: Touch, say, and stop at five
weeks.objective: Count objects through 5 with one spoken number per object and tell how many.

connection.before: Use everyday touching, moving, and spoken words; reading and written arithmetic are not prerequisites.
connection.after: Represent quantities 0–5 with objects, drawings, spoken words, and numerals.

days: Count one to three counters with an adult, then try four and five.
Study the row model and practise moving counted objects on sheet A.
Match fingers, dots, and counters using sheet B.
Act out selected picnic and puppet tasks on sheet C.
Show a fresh collection of up to five and explain how each object was counted once.
explanation: An adult reads every direction. Place a few counters where they can move freely. Touch or slide one counter while saying one number word: one, two, three. A number word belongs to one object, even when one object is larger than another. Start with collections of one to three and extend to five when ready.

After touching the last counter, repeat the last number to answer how many. That number describes the whole collection, not only the final object. Show the same quantity with fingers or a drawing. An adult may record the numeral; accurate counting matters more than neat writing in this first week.

Moving a counted counter to a separate space helps keep track. If a counter is touched twice or a word is skipped, start again slowly and move each object once. A spoken count can sound smooth and still be wrong if the words and objects do not match.

examples.prompt: An adult puts 3 counters in a row. Show how to count the whole row.
steps: Point to the first counter and say one.
Move along the row, saying two and three once each.
The last word is three, so the whole row has 3 counters.

examples.prompt: Two spoons lie on a table. How can fingers show how many spoons there are?
steps: Touch one spoon and say one.
Touch the other spoon and say two.
Raise one finger for each spoon; 2 fingers match the 2 spoons.

worksheets.title: Build and point: Touch, say, and stop at five
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: Place 1 counter on paper. Touch it and tell how many.
steps: Touch the only counter once.
The count ends at one, so there is 1.

items.prompt: Draw a dot, another dot, and another dot. Count your dots aloud.
steps: Touch each of the three drawn dots.
Say one, two, three; three names the whole set.

items.prompt: An adult taps the table twice, slowly. Put down one counter for each tap. How many counters?
steps: Place a counter after the first tap and another after the second.
Count the counters: one, two.

items.prompt: Place 4 counters in a line. Slide each to a new line while counting. How many moved?
steps: Move each of the four counters once.
The last count word is four.

items.prompt: Hold up 5 fingers on one hand. Touch each with your other hand and count.
steps: Match one spoken number to each finger.
Stop after five because every finger was touched.

items.prompt: An adult sets out 2 blocks and 1 spoon. Count all the objects without sorting them.
steps: Count each block once, then the spoon once.
Different kinds still belong to the same collection of 3.

worksheets.title: Draw and explain: Touch, say, and stop at five
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: Make a collection that matches 4 fingers held up by an adult.
steps: Give one counter to each raised finger.
All four fingers have one counter each.

items.prompt: Put 5 dots on paper, then cover each with one counter. How many counters did you use?
steps: Cover each dot once without covering a dot twice.
Five covered dots need 5 counters.

items.prompt: An adult places 3 counters far apart. Point to every counter once. Tell the total.
steps: Touch the separated counters one at a time.
Spacing does not stop the count at three.

items.prompt: A child touches 2 counters and says one, two, three, using two words on the last counter. Show a repair.
items.answer: Say one, two; there are 2 counters.
steps: Give the first counter only one count word.
Give the second only two, then stop.

items.prompt: Draw 1 circle to stand for a toy car. How many cars does your picture show?
steps: One circle stands for one car.
Count the single circle to find 1.

items.prompt: Build a row of 4 counters. Point to the last counter, then sweep your hand over the whole row. What does four tell?
items.answer: There are 4 in the whole row.
steps: Count all four once.
The last word tells the size of the entire collection.

worksheets.title: Use and check: Touch, say, and stop at five
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: Pretend 3 counters are picnic guests. Put one paper dot beside each as a cup. How many cups?
steps: Match one drawn cup to each guest.
Three guests have 3 matching cups.

items.prompt: An adult holds up 2 fingers, then lowers them. Show the same amount with dots.
steps: Remember one dot for each of the two fingers.
Count the drawing to check two.

items.prompt: Count these spoken names as objects: hat, sock, boot, coat. Move a counter for each. How many objects were named?
steps: Move one counter for each of the four names.
Counting the moved counters ends at four.

items.prompt: Place 5 counters in a little pile. Move them into a counted row. Tell how moving helped.
items.answer: 5; moving separated counted and uncounted counters.
steps: Take just one counter at a time from the pile.
The completed row contains all five without repeats.

items.prompt: A puppet counts 3 blocks as one, three, four. Count correctly for the puppet.
steps: The number after one is two.
Give the last block the word three.

items.prompt: Choose 1, 2, 3, 4, or 5 counters for a pretend treasure. Count and tell an adult your total.
items.answer: Any chosen total from 1 to 5, correctly matched to the counters.
steps: Move every chosen counter once.
The stated total must match the final count word.

weeks.title: Zero and number labels
weeks.objective: Represent quantities 0–5 with objects, drawings, spoken words, and numerals.

connection.before: Count objects through 5 with one spoken number per object and tell how many.
connection.after: Count sets through 10, keeping track in lines and scattered arrangements.

days: Compare an empty plate with a plate holding one counter.
Read numeral cards 0–5 together and build sheet A collections.
Draw amounts and practise comfortable numeral formation on sheet B.
Use selected tray and garden tasks from sheet C.
Match an adult-read numeral to a new set and explain zero without a picture cue.
explanation: Zero names a collection with no objects. Draw a plate and leave it empty, then put one counter on another plate. Say zero for the empty plate and one for the plate with a counter. An empty space is a meaningful amount, so it can have a number label too.

An adult writes numeral cards 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 and reads them aloud. Build each amount beneath its card, touching objects to check. Trace or copy the numeral after its quantity makes sense. A child may point to a card or dictate while an adult writes.

The numeral is a label for how many; its size on the paper does not tell the amount. A large written 2 still means two objects. Separate counting accuracy from handwriting: if a numeral is reversed or difficult to form, ask the child to show its quantity before helping with the mark.

examples.prompt: An empty nest drawing has no eggs. Which label, 0 or 3, belongs beside it?
steps: Look inside the nest for any eggs.
There are no eggs to touch or count.
Choose 0 because zero records no eggs.

examples.prompt: Make a picture for the numeral 4.
steps: Read the numeral as four with an adult.
Draw four dots while saying one, two, three, four.
Touch the finished dots to check that the label matches all four.

worksheets.title: Build and point: Zero and number labels
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: Draw an empty bowl. An adult offers cards 0 and 2. Point to its number label.
steps: The bowl contains no counters.
Zero is the label for none.

items.prompt: An adult writes 3. Place that many counters underneath it.
steps: Read the card as three.
Count out three counters and stop.

items.prompt: Place 5 counters by a plate drawing. Choose between adult-read labels 1 and 5.
steps: Count the counters once.
The last word five matches the label 5.

items.prompt: An adult draws 2 dots. Copy or point to their numeral from 0, 2, 4.
steps: Count one and two while touching the dots.
Select the symbol read as two.

items.prompt: Put 1 counter in a drawn box and leave a second box empty. Label both orally.
steps: The first box has a single object.
The second has none, which is zero.

items.prompt: Draw a large 4 and a tiny 4 with adult help. Build what each means.
steps: Both marks are read four.
The size of the written mark does not change the quantity.

worksheets.title: Draw and explain: Zero and number labels
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: An adult labels a drawing of 3 stars with 5. Correct the label by pointing or writing.
steps: Count the stars: one, two, three.
Use the label that matches the count.

items.prompt: Write or trace 0 beside a cup with no pretend juice counters. Explain the zero.
items.answer: Zero means there are no juice counters.
steps: Look for counters inside the cup drawing.
None are there, so the label is 0.

items.prompt: Make 2 counters and 2 pencil dots. Give both collections a numeral label.
steps: Count each collection separately.
Both counts end at two.

items.prompt: An adult reads cards 1, 3, and 5. Choose a card and draw the amount without copying another picture.
items.answer: A matching drawing of 1, 3, or 5 objects.
steps: Read the chosen numeral aloud.
Count the drawing to confirm its label.

items.prompt: Place 4 counters in a square arrangement. An adult reads labels 4 and 0. Choose and explain.
steps: Touch the four counters in turn.
Zero would mean no counters.

items.prompt: A puppet says an empty plate cannot have a number. Tell or show why it can.
steps: Show that the plate has no objects.
Zero records that empty collection.

worksheets.title: Use and check: Zero and number labels
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: For a pretend shop, label a tray holding 1 button and another holding 3 buttons.
steps: Touch the button in the first tray.
Count three in the second, then match both labels.

items.prompt: Draw 5 pretend raindrops. Ask an adult to write your dictated numeral beside them.
steps: Give every raindrop one count word.
The final word five names the drawing's amount.

items.prompt: An adult writes cards 0, 2, and 4. Make a treasure tray for the middle card as displayed: 0, 2, 4.
steps: The middle card is read two.
Count out two objects for that card.

items.prompt: A drawn garden is labeled 0 flowers. What should be inside it? Show the garden.
steps: Read zero as no flowers.
Leave the garden empty rather than drawing one flower.

items.prompt: An adult writes 5 beneath a row of 4 buttons. Without changing buttons, fix the record.
steps: Count the existing buttons to four.
The record must describe the unchanged collection.

items.prompt: Choose one empty collection and one collection of 1 to 5 counters. Show their labels and explain.
items.answer: 0 for the empty collection and a matching numeral 1–5 for the other.
steps: Check that the first space is empty.
Count the other set once and select its numeral.

weeks.title: Count to ten without losing objects
weeks.objective: Count sets through 10, keeping track in lines and scattered arrangements.

connection.before: Represent quantities 0–5 with objects, drawings, spoken words, and numerals.
connection.after: Explain that rearranging a counted set through 10 preserves its total.

days: Echo the count from one through ten while moving counters.
Model a scattered collection and use sheet A to connect counts to labels.
Try row and ring tracking methods on sheet B.
Use bus and flower tasks to discuss what counts as one object.
Count a new scattered set of no more than ten and explain the tracking choice.
explanation: Extend the familiar count through five by saying six, seven, eight, nine, ten as counters join a line. An adult can say the sequence first and the child can echo it. Counting larger sets still uses the same rule: touch or move one object for each spoken number.

In a scattered collection, the eyes alone may lose track. Move counted objects onto a separate sheet, or draw a small mark beside each pictured object after touching it. The final count word tells the total. Match the total to an adult-read numeral from 6 through 10.

Do not count empty spaces or jump back to objects already counted. If the count changes on a second try, use a clearer arrangement and count again. Two rows may help the eyes follow the objects, but each counter is still counted individually rather than assuming the rows have equal amounts.

examples.prompt: An adult places 7 counters in a loose cluster. Count them reliably.
steps: Choose an empty space for counted counters.
Move each counter once, saying one through seven.
The original space is empty and the new space holds all 7.

examples.prompt: An adult draws 5 dots in a top row and 3 below. Count every dot.
steps: Touch the top row while saying one through five.
Continue with six, seven, eight on the bottom row.
Stop at eight after touching every dot exactly once.

worksheets.title: Build and point: Count to ten without losing objects
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: Place 6 counters in a row and count them. Copy or point to an adult-written 6.
steps: Say one through six as you touch the row.
The count and numeral both name six.

items.prompt: An adult scatters 8 counters. Move each to a paper circle while counting.
steps: Only move counters that are still outside the circle.
The last moved counter gets the word eight.

items.prompt: Draw 4 dots on top and 5 below. Count all the dots with a finger.
steps: Count the four top dots first.
Continue five through nine on the lower row.

items.prompt: An adult reads 10 from a card. Make exactly that many pretend stepping stones with counters.
steps: Put down one counter for each word one through ten.
Stop at ten and recount the finished path.

items.prompt: Put 7 counters in a curved line. Tell how many without straightening them.
steps: Start at one end of the curve.
Follow the curve, touching each counter once to seven.

items.prompt: An adult writes 6, 8, and 9. Match a collection of 8 paper dots to its label.
steps: Count the eight dots once.
Point to the numeral read as eight.

worksheets.title: Draw and explain: Count to ten without losing objects
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: A puppet counts 6 blocks as one, two, three, four, five, seven. Repair the last word.
items.answer: The last word should be six; 6 blocks.
steps: Keep the first five count words.
The next word after five is six.

items.prompt: Draw a row of 3 dots and another row of 3 dots. Count across both rows.
steps: Count the first row one, two, three.
Continue four, five, six on the second row.

items.prompt: Put 9 counters in a ring. Choose a starting counter and move it aside. Count it first and finish the ring.
steps: Count the moved counter as one to mark the start.
Touch the remaining eight once and stop at nine.

items.prompt: An adult puts 10 counters in a pile. Explain a way to keep counted ones separate, then use it.
items.answer: 10; move counted counters into a new row or space.
steps: Select an empty destination.
Move and count each object once until the pile is empty.

items.prompt: Read these number words aloud with an adult: five, six, blank, eight. Say the missing word.
steps: After five comes six.
The word between six and eight is seven.

items.prompt: Draw 7 dots in any arrangement and label them with adult help.
steps: Count while making the dots.
Recount the finished drawing to match the label.

worksheets.title: Use and check: Count to ten without losing objects
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: A pretend bus needs 6 passengers. Start with an empty bus drawing and place the passengers.
steps: Place one counter for each passenger.
Stop when the count reaches six.

items.prompt: An adult says eight but writes 9 for a counted collection. Which record matches the spoken total?
steps: The spoken total is eight.
The numeral 9 says nine and does not match.

items.prompt: Make 10 counters into two rows, one of 4 and one of 6. Count all without restarting at one in the second row.
steps: Say one through four on the first row.
Continue five through ten on the six remaining objects.

items.prompt: A child touches 9 counters but touches one of them twice and says ten. Show how to check.
steps: Move each counter to a counted space.
No object can receive two count words there.

items.prompt: An adult draws 8 flowers as circles with stems. Count flowers, not circles and stems separately.
steps: Each circle with its attached stem is one flower.
Count one word per whole flower to eight.

items.prompt: Choose a number from 6 to 10. Make its collection and tell the adult how to check it.
items.answer: Any matching set of 6–10 counters with one-to-one checking.
steps: State the chosen amount before building.
A second count must end at that same amount.

weeks.title: Same set, new arrangement
weeks.objective: Explain that rearranging a counted set through 10 preserves its total.

connection.before: Count sets through 10, keeping track in lines and scattered arrangements.
connection.after: Count from a given number and represent arranged quantities and numerals through 20.

days: Compare a tight row with a spread row of the same counters.
Use sheet A to practise location words while tracking totals.
Draw one-to-one matches and discuss the puppet claim on sheet B.
Act out changes that do and do not change the collection on sheet C.
Explain a new rearrangement using the words added none and removed none.
explanation: Count a small collection, then slide the same counters into a different arrangement. Nothing has entered or left. Count again to see that the total is unchanged. A longer row can contain the same number of counters when the gaps are larger; length of a row and number in the row are different ideas.

Use above, below, beside, and between to describe where counters sit relative to a drawn box or one another. These position words tell location rather than quantity. When counters move from above a box to below it, ask separately where they are and how many there are.

A useful explanation names what stayed the same: we moved all the objects, added none, and removed none. If a counter is actually added or taken away, recount; that is a changed collection. Encourage children to demonstrate with objects before asking for a spoken reason.

examples.prompt: Count 6 counters in a short row. Spread the same 6 into a long row. How many now?
steps: Count the short row to six.
Slide the counters apart without adding or removing any.
The same six remain; recounting the long row confirms 6.

examples.prompt: Put 3 counters above a drawn box, then move all of them below it. Describe the result.
steps: Count three counters above the box.
Move each of those same counters to below the box.
The position changed, but no counter entered or left, so the count stays 3.

worksheets.title: Build and point: Same set, new arrangement
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: Count 4 counters in a row, then move them into a square. How many are in the square arrangement?
steps: The row starts with four objects.
Only their places change, so the total stays four.

items.prompt: Put 5 counters beside a cup drawing. Move the cup drawing, not the counters. How many counters remain?
steps: Count the counters before moving the paper.
Moving the reference picture changes no counters.

items.prompt: An adult puts 7 counters in a tight group. Spread them without adding any. Does the count grow?
steps: Wider gaps use more space.
The number of objects is unchanged.

items.prompt: Place 2 counters above a paper line and move both below it. Tell where and how many.
steps: Both original counters move below.
There are still two counters to count.

items.prompt: A row has 8 counters. Start counting at the other end. What total should you get?
steps: Every counter is touched once whichever end starts the count.
The same set therefore ends at eight.

items.prompt: Arrange 3 counters with one between the other two. Tell the total and point to between.
items.answer: 3 counters; the middle counter is between the other two.
steps: Touch all three to count.
Point to the counter that has one neighbor on each side.

worksheets.title: Draw and explain: Same set, new arrangement
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: Draw 6 dots close together on one paper. On another, draw a matching dot for each far apart. Compare totals.
steps: Match one new dot to each original dot.
Spacing changes, but six matches preserve the total.

items.prompt: A puppet says 5 counters became 7 when they spread out. Explain the mistake without adding counters.
items.answer: There are still 5; gaps are not counters.
steps: Touch each actual counter once.
Count objects rather than the empty spaces between them.

items.prompt: Make a ring of 9 counters. Move the same counters into a line and label its count.
steps: Move every ring counter to the line once.
No counters are added or lost, so the label is nine.

items.prompt: Place 1 counter inside a drawn box. Move it outside. Did the amount of counters on the whole paper change?
steps: The counter changed location within the paper.
The whole paper still holds the same object.

items.prompt: Count 10 counters on a mat. An adult shifts all ten to the left side. Say the new total.
steps: Count the original mat collection to ten.
Shifting the entire set preserves every object.

items.prompt: Draw a box and place 4 counters below it. Give an instruction that moves them without changing their number.
items.answer: For example, move all 4 above the box; other moves preserving all four are valid.
steps: Choose a new location for the same counters.
Check that four moved and none were added.

worksheets.title: Use and check: Same set, new arrangement
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: A pretend shop spreads 6 buttons to fill a shelf. It started with 6 and adds none. Does it have more to sell?
steps: Selling amount depends on buttons, not shelf space.
Recounting the same six confirms the quantity.

items.prompt: Count 7 toy dots in a circle. An adult adds 1 new dot. Is this only a rearrangement?
steps: A new object entered the collection.
Counting all the dots gives eight rather than seven.

items.prompt: A child counts 4 counters, then hides 1 under paper without removing it from the table. How many table counters exist, including the hidden one?
steps: Three are visible and one is covered.
Covering does not remove a counter from the collection.

items.prompt: Make 8 paper marks for birds. Move the paper upside down. How many birds are shown?
steps: Turning the whole drawing changes direction.
The same eight bird marks remain.

items.prompt: Place 3 counters beside a box and then put all inside it. Explain two facts that are true now.
items.answer: There are 3 counters, and they are inside the box.
steps: Count the same three after the move.
Use inside to describe their new position.

items.prompt: Arrange 5 counters twice in very different ways. Tell how you know both arrangements have the same count.
items.answer: Both have 5 because the same five counters were moved.
steps: Count the original five once.
Show that no counters entered or left during the move.

weeks.title: Count on and record through twenty
weeks.objective: Count from a given number and represent arranged quantities and numerals through 20.

connection.before: Explain that rearranging a counted set through 10 preserves its total.
connection.after: Choose reliable counting methods, record 0–20, and begin an oral count beyond twenty.

days: Say ten through twenty together and connect each word to an added counter.
Study continuing-count and arranged-collection models, then use sheet A.
Record teen numerals with adult support and repair a sequence on sheet B.
Apply counting to organized seats and tickets on sheet C.
Count a new arranged set through twenty and continue a separate count from a supplied number.
explanation: Extend the oral count from ten through twenty slowly with adult support. The teen names may sound alike, so pair each word with the next object in an orderly row. For collections larger than ten, use rows or a simple rectangle; keep scattered counting collections to ten or fewer.

To continue from a given number, say that number and then its next neighbors. Starting at twelve does not require returning to one. A numeral label can help the adult show where the spoken sequence begins. Count a whole collection separately when the question asks for how many objects.

Read and write numerals 11–20 with an adult, connecting each to a counted collection. Copying a numeral alone does not show its meaning. For now, count each object; later lessons will organize teen amounts as ten and extra ones. Pay attention to the order of the two written digits.

examples.prompt: An adult says twelve. Continue the count through sixteen.
steps: Begin with the supplied number twelve.
Say the next numbers in order: thirteen, fourteen, fifteen.
Finish with sixteen without returning to one.

examples.prompt: An adult makes 2 rows of counters, 10 in the top row and 4 below. Count all and label them.
steps: Count the top row one through ten.
Continue eleven, twelve, thirteen, fourteen on the lower row.
The last number is fourteen, written 14 with adult help.

worksheets.title: Build and point: Count on and record through twenty
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: Start at 6 and count aloud through 10, with an adult pointing to numeral cards.
steps: Begin at the supplied six.
Continue to each next number until ten.

items.prompt: Make a row of 10 counters with 1 more below. Count every counter and choose adult-read 11 or 12.
steps: Count the first row through ten.
The last counter is eleven, matching 11.

items.prompt: An adult lays 3 rows of 5 counters. Count by ones and tell the total.
steps: Count the first row one through five and the second six through ten.
Count the last row eleven through fifteen.

items.prompt: An adult reads 18. Make 18 dots in neat rows, then trace or copy the numeral.
steps: Count one new dot for each number through eighteen.
Recount the completed rows before labeling.

items.prompt: Say the numbers missing here: 9, 10, blank, blank, 13.
steps: After ten comes eleven.
Twelve follows eleven and comes before thirteen.

items.prompt: An adult places 2 rows of 10 counters. Count by ones, then tell which label fits: 12 or 20.
steps: Count the first row one through ten.
Continue eleven through twenty on the second.

worksheets.title: Draw and explain: Count on and record through twenty
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: Begin at 13 and say the next 3 numbers after it.
steps: Fourteen is the first number after thirteen.
Fifteen and sixteen complete three next numbers.

items.prompt: Draw 10 dots in a row and 2 below. Count and dictate the number label.
steps: Count the top row to ten.
The two lower dots receive eleven and twelve.

items.prompt: A puppet says sixteen, seventeen, nineteen, twenty. Supply the missing word.
steps: The number after seventeen is eighteen.
Nineteen comes after eighteen.

items.prompt: Build 17 counters in two rows. An adult reads 17 and 7. Point to the correct card.
steps: Count all seventeen counters once.
Seven would stop too soon and leave ten uncounted.
items.skill: Distinguishing a teen from a single digit

items.prompt: An adult draws 10 circles in a row and 3 in another row. Touch each and write or dictate the total.
steps: The first row ends at ten.
Continue eleven, twelve, thirteen on the second row.

items.prompt: An adult writes 19. Say it together, then show its amount with organized counters.
steps: Read the numeral as nineteen.
Count out one counter per word through nineteen.

worksheets.title: Use and check: Count on and record through twenty
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: Pretend there are 16 seats, drawn as 2 rows of 8 dots. Place one passenger counter on each. Count the passengers.
steps: Match a counter to every seat once.
Counting all occupied seats ends at sixteen.

items.prompt: At a pretend parade, the adult has counted through 14. Say 15 through 20 without starting again.
steps: The next count word after fourteen is fifteen.
Continue one word at a time to twenty.

items.prompt: A label says 11 tickets but the arranged drawing has 10 dots above and 5 below. Correct the label.
steps: Count ten in the first row and continue through fifteen below.
The total is fifteen, not eleven.

items.prompt: Count 20 counters in a rectangle of 4 rows of 5. Explain how to avoid counting a row twice.
items.answer: 20; complete each row once in a fixed order.
steps: Count across the first row, then move to the next.
Four completed rows account for all twenty counters.

items.prompt: An adult says nineteen, then asks for the next number. Show that number with 2 rows of counters.
items.answer: Twenty; 20 counters, for example 10 in each row.
steps: Twenty follows nineteen.
Count the drawn or placed counters to twenty.

items.prompt: Choose 12, 14, or 18 from adult-read cards. Draw that amount in rows and explain your count.
items.answer: A row drawing matching the chosen 12, 14, or 18.
steps: Count each row in order without restarting.
The last number must match the chosen card.

weeks.title: A counting workshop
weeks.objective: Choose reliable counting methods, record 0–20, and begin an oral count beyond twenty.

connection.before: Count from a given number and represent arranged quantities and numerals through 20.
connection.after: Compare two collections through 10 by pairing objects and naming more, fewer, or equal.

days: Choose tracking methods for lines, circles, and scattered sets.
Use sheet A to reconnect numerals, objects, and location language.
Extend the oral sequence to thirty with adult modeling; practise selected sheet B tasks.
Present a garden or collection challenge from sheet C.
Give a short oral demonstration: count, label, rearrange, and explain what stayed the same.
explanation: Use this week to choose a method, not to race. A line can be counted from one end, a scattered set can be moved, and a ring needs a marked starting place. Count scattered sets only through ten and arranged sets through twenty. Explain why each method prevents skips or double counts.

Read numeral labels 0–20 with an adult and make matching objects or drawings. Include zero in the choices. If a drawing and its label disagree, recount the drawing before changing either. A written record should describe the actual collection, including objects that are temporarily covered.

Begin extending the oral count through thirty: after twenty come twenty-one through twenty-nine, then thirty. An adult models this language and supplies the numeral sequence when needed. This oral extension does not require counting a scattered set of thirty; larger oral counts continue later in the course.

examples.prompt: An adult puts 9 counters around a paper circle. How can you count them without passing the start twice?
steps: Move the first counter just outside the circle and count it as one.
Follow the remaining counters once, saying two through nine.
Stop before the marked starting place; all nine were counted once.

examples.prompt: Continue this adult-read count: 26, 27, 28, blank, blank.
steps: Listen to the sequence twenty-six, twenty-seven, twenty-eight.
Twenty-nine follows twenty-eight.
After twenty-nine, the next number is thirty.

worksheets.title: Build and point: A counting workshop
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: Count 8 scattered counters by moving them to a new space. Tell why this method works.
steps: Move one counter for each word.
The original space empties without repeating an object.

items.prompt: Make an arranged collection for adult-read numeral 16 and label it.
steps: Count out sixteen objects in rows.
The final spoken number matches the written label.

items.prompt: An adult draws a box with no objects inside and 4 dots outside. Give the inside count.
steps: Only objects inside the box belong to this requested set.
There are none there, so the inside count is zero.

items.prompt: Say the next number in each adult-read pair: 17, blank; 19, blank.
steps: Eighteen follows seventeen.
Twenty follows nineteen.

items.prompt: Arrange 10 counters in a ring, then in a zigzag. Explain whether the total changes.
steps: Count the original ten.
Rearrangement keeps every counter and adds none.

items.prompt: An adult writes 12 and 21 and reads both. Point to twelve and build it in rows.
steps: Choose the numeral whose first digit is 1 and second is 2.
Count twelve counters to confirm its meaning.

worksheets.title: Draw and explain: A counting workshop
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: A puppet counts a row of 7 counters but skips the middle counter. What should it do before recording a total?
items.answer: Recount all seven, touching each once; record 7.
steps: The skipped object has not received a count word.
A complete second count ends at seven.

items.prompt: Continue aloud from 21 through 25 with adult support.
steps: Begin at twenty-one.
Keep the twenty part and advance the final words through five.

items.prompt: Draw 19 dots in neat rows and circle the last dot you counted. Does nineteen name only that dot?
steps: Each earlier dot received a count word too.
The final word tells the whole collection's size.

items.prompt: Place 6 counters below a paper line. Move 2 of those counters above the line. How many are on the whole paper?
steps: Moving within the paper does not remove any.
Count both locations as one whole collection.

items.prompt: An adult presents cards 0, 5, 10, and 15. Make a collection for any one and explain the match.
items.answer: A matching collection for the chosen 0, 5, 10, or 15.
steps: Read the selected card with the adult.
Check the collection by one-to-one counting, or show none for zero.

items.prompt: Count 20 drawn dots arranged as 5 rows of 4. Describe where you start and stop.
items.answer: 20 dots; start at the first row and finish at the last dot of the fifth row.
steps: Count each row left to right in order.
Continue the count across rows until twenty.

worksheets.title: Use and check: A counting workshop
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: A pretend garden plan needs 13 seeds. Draw an organized seed picture and dictate its label.
steps: Make one dot for each number through thirteen.
Recount all dots before giving the label.

items.prompt: A collector spreads 9 stones and says the collection is bigger now. Explain what bigger could mean and what stayed the same.
items.answer: It uses more space, but still has 9 stones.
steps: The gaps can grow without new stones.
Counting objects still ends at nine.

items.prompt: Start at 28 and continue through 30, following an adult's numeral cards.
steps: Twenty-nine follows twenty-eight.
Thirty begins the next group of count words.

items.prompt: A tray label says 18. Its drawing has 10 dots above and 7 below. Keep the dots and repair the record.
steps: Count the ten top dots, then eleven through seventeen below.
The drawing's total is seventeen.

items.prompt: An adult puts 5 counters beside a drawn tent and covers all five with paper. How many counters are still beside the tent?
steps: All five stayed in the same collection.
Covering changes visibility rather than quantity.

items.prompt: Make a counting challenge for an adult with 0–10 counters. Show a reliable checking method and its total.
items.answer: Any accurately counted set from 0 to 10 with an appropriate check.
steps: Arrange or move the counters so each is tracked once.
An empty set is zero; otherwise report the last count word.

weeks.title: Match to compare
weeks.objective: Compare two collections through 10 by pairing objects and naming more, fewer, or equal.

connection.before: Choose reliable counting methods, record 0–20, and begin an oral count beyond twenty.
connection.after: Compare adult-read numerals 1–10 by building, matching, and counting their amounts.

days: Pair small collections and name the leftover group.
Study both models, then practise sheet A comparisons.
Use sheet B to repair unfair pairings and make equal groups.
Act out shortages using selected sheet C tasks.
Compare two new sets and explain both more and fewer directions.
explanation: Place one counter from each collection together to make a pair. Continue until one collection runs out. If both collections end together, they have equal numbers. If one has unpaired objects, it has more; the other has fewer. No comparison symbols are needed.

A comparison describes a relationship between two named groups. Say more cups than plates rather than just more. A larger object does not count as several smaller objects: a large pretend cup matches one plate just as a small cup does. Use counters or simple drawings as stand-ins.

Check a pairing by counting both sets separately. Matching is especially helpful when objects are spread differently, because visual length can mislead. Every object must belong to only one pair; sharing a partner hides a shortage. Use quantities through ten and let the child explain by pointing.

examples.prompt: There are 4 pretend cups and 6 pretend plates. Which collection has more?
examples.answer: Plates have more; cups have fewer.
steps: Make four cup-and-plate pairs.
Two plates remain without cups.
The leftover plates show that the six plates are more than four cups.

examples.prompt: Pair 3 large button counters with 3 small dot drawings. Are the amounts equal?
steps: Match one button with one dot.
All three buttons and all three dots have partners.
Size differs, but equal pairing proves equal numbers.

worksheets.title: Build and point: Match to compare
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: Draw 2 hats and 3 heads as circles. Pair one hat to each head. Which group has more?
steps: Two hats match two heads.
One head has no hat.

items.prompt: Put 5 counters in each of two rows. Pair across rows and describe the amounts.
steps: Each counter in one row gets one partner.
Neither row has leftovers.

items.prompt: Model 6 bowls and 4 spoons with two kinds of marks. Which group has fewer?
steps: Four spoon marks pair with four bowls.
Two bowls remain unmatched.

items.prompt: Set 1 large paper circle beside 2 small paper circles. Which group has more objects?
steps: Count the large circle as one object.
Two small circles make a larger count despite smaller size.

items.prompt: Make 7 counters in a close row and 5 in a wide row. Pair them. Which has more?
steps: Five pairs use all five wide-row counters.
Two close-row counters remain.

items.prompt: Show 4 drawn flowers and 4 counter bees. Does every flower get exactly one bee?
steps: Match each bee to a different flower.
Four pairs use both collections completely.

worksheets.title: Draw and explain: Match to compare
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: An adult draws 8 seats and 6 passenger dots. Explain whether each seat gets a passenger.
steps: Match six passengers to six different seats.
Two of the eight seats remain empty.

items.prompt: Draw lines pairing 3 triangles with 5 circles. Name both comparison directions.
items.answer: Fewer triangles than circles; more circles than triangles.
steps: Three pairs use every triangle.
Two circles remain, identifying the larger collection.

items.prompt: A puppet pairs 2 counters to the same dot and calls 4 counters equal to 3 dots. Repair the pairs.
steps: Give each dot only one counter.
One counter remains after three fair pairs.

items.prompt: Build two equal collections using a total of 6 counters, sharing one at a time.
steps: Alternate placing counters into the two collections.
Three pairs use all six.

items.prompt: Choose the group with fewer: 9 drawn stars or 7 drawn moons. Model if useful.
steps: Pair seven stars with the seven moons.
Two stars remain beyond the pairs.

items.prompt: Make 2 equal groups with 2 counters in each. Spread one group. Are the groups still equal?
steps: Moving counters does not add any.
Each still has two matching partners.

worksheets.title: Use and check: Match to compare
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: There are 5 pretend puppies and 3 blankets. Use counters to show whether one blanket per puppy is possible.
steps: Match three blankets to three puppies.
Two puppies remain unmatched.

items.prompt: An adult makes 4 dot tickets and 6 circle guests. Tell which group needs more partners.
items.answer: Guests need tickets; 2 guests lack them.
steps: Match one ticket to one guest.
Only four guests can receive tickets.

items.prompt: Draw a group with more than 2 but no more than 5 objects. Explain your choice.
steps: Pair two of its objects with a two-counter reference group.
At least one object remains, proving more.

items.prompt: Draw a group with fewer than 4 but at least 1 object. Check by matching.
steps: Pair its objects with counters from a four-counter set.
The set of four has leftovers.

items.prompt: A pretend shop has 10 cups and 10 lids. Explain why no lid is left over after fair matching.
items.answer: There are equal amounts, so all 10 pairs are complete.
steps: Give each cup a different lid.
All ten cups and lids are used once.

items.prompt: Make two collections of your choice, each no bigger than 5. Tell more, fewer, or equal and prove it.
items.answer: Any accurate comparison with one-to-one pairs.
steps: Pair one item from each group until one runs out.
Leftovers show more; no leftovers show equal.

weeks.title: Numbers can compare collections
weeks.objective: Compare adult-read numerals 1–10 by building, matching, and counting their amounts.

connection.before: Compare two collections through 10 by pairing objects and naming more, fewer, or equal.
connection.after: Identify circles, triangles, squares, rectangles, and hexagons by features across size and orientation.

days: Connect paired collections to numeral cards 1–10.
Practise full comparison sentences with sheet A.
Use counting order and repair printed-size reasoning on sheet B.
Apply numeral comparisons to pretend labels on sheet C.
Compare two new numeral cards and justify with counters or an oral sequence.
explanation: A written numeral can stand for a whole collection. Read two numeral cards with an adult, build their amounts, and pair the counters. The card for the group with leftovers names the greater number; the other names the smaller number. Greater means more objects, not a larger printed mark.

In the counting sequence, a number reached later names a greater quantity when each next word adds one object. Practise brief sequences from a supplied number through ten. Link the sequence to the collections rather than relying only on a memorized comparison phrase.

Use words greater than, less than, and equal to; formal inequality symbols are optional adult records. Reversing the order of the cards reverses the wording: eight is greater than six, and six is less than eight. Two identical numerals describe equal counts even when drawn in different sizes.

examples.prompt: An adult reads cards 8 and 6. Which number is greater?
steps: Build eight counters and six counters.
Make six pairs, leaving two counters in the eight group.
The group with leftovers is greater, so choose 8.

examples.prompt: Compare a large printed 3 with a small printed 3.
steps: Read both numeral cards as three.
Build three counters for each card.
Three pairs use both groups completely, so printed size does not matter.

worksheets.title: Build and point: Numbers can compare collections
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: An adult reads 2 and 5. Build both amounts and name the greater numeral.
steps: Pair two objects from each group.
The five group has three leftovers.

items.prompt: Listen to 7 and 4. Which numeral names fewer counters? Show it.
steps: Build seven counters and four counters.
The four group runs out first in pairing.

items.prompt: An adult writes 6 twice with different colors. Compare their amounts.
steps: Both cards are read six.
Six pairs match all objects in both groups.

items.prompt: Count aloud from 3 through 6. Which is greater, the starting number or ending number?
steps: The count passes four and five to reach six.
A six-object set contains more objects than three.

items.prompt: An adult reads 9 and 10. Model both and choose the smaller.
steps: Nine pairs fit within the ten group.
One counter remains only in the ten group.

items.prompt: Build collections for adult-read 1 and 8. Say a complete less-than sentence.
steps: Only one pair can be made.
The eight group still has seven counters.

worksheets.title: Draw and explain: Numbers can compare collections
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: A puppet says 4 is greater than 7 because its printed card is taller. Correct it.
steps: Count out the quantities named by each numeral.
Seven counters outnumber four regardless of card height.

items.prompt: An adult shows 5 then 2. Say greater than; then reverse the cards and say less than.
items.answer: 5 is greater than 2; 2 is less than 5.
steps: The same two quantities keep their sizes.
Changing their order changes which comparison phrase fits.

items.prompt: Choose an adult-read numeral from 1, 4, 8 that names more than 6.
steps: One and four come before six and name smaller sets.
Eight leaves counters after pairing with six.

items.prompt: Find the equal pair among adult-read pairs 2 and 3; 7 and 7; 6 and 9.
steps: Equal numerals name equal counts.
The other pairs have different quantities.

items.prompt: An adult counts five, six, seven, eight. Compare 5 and 8 with a drawing.
steps: Draw five dots and eight dots.
Pairing leaves three dots only in the eight group.

items.prompt: Choose a numeral 1–10 smaller than 3 and build it.
steps: Build the chosen amount.
Pair with three counters to show that three has leftovers.

worksheets.title: Use and check: Numbers can compare collections
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: Two pretend stands display adult-read signs 6 balloons and 9 balloons. Which has more balloons?
steps: Represent each sign with dots.
Nine dots include three more than six.

items.prompt: A game needs a card greater than 7. The adult reads 4, 8, 6. Which card works?
steps: Build or count the three amounts.
Only eight comes after seven and exceeds it.

items.prompt: A toy bus sign says 5 seats and another says 5 seats. Are their seat counts different if one bus drawing is bigger?
steps: The labels specify five each.
Picture size does not change the stated quantities.

items.prompt: A child labels 3 counters with 8 and then says 8 is less than 4. Explain how to fix the starting record.
items.answer: Label the three counters 3; then 3 is less than 4.
steps: The label 8 does not match the three objects.
A correct comparison must start with correct quantities.

items.prompt: Choose two different adult-read numerals 1–10. Build them and tell which is greater.
items.answer: Any correct comparison of the chosen different numerals.
steps: Count each collection separately.
Pair them; the group with leftovers names the greater numeral.

items.prompt: Which adult-read label is between 2 and 4 in the counting sequence: 1, 3, or 5?
steps: Say two, three, four in order.
Three follows two and comes before four.

weeks.title: Flat shapes keep their names
weeks.objective: Identify circles, triangles, squares, rectangles, and hexagons by features across size and orientation.

connection.before: Compare adult-read numerals 1–10 by building, matching, and counting their amounts.
connection.after: Distinguish flat shapes from solids and identify sphere, cube, cone, and cylinder models.

days: Trace adult-drawn shapes and count their sides and corners.
Use sheet A to recognize shapes in different directions and sizes.
Compare defining features and nonexamples on sheet B.
Make and describe original shape pictures with sheet C.
Identify a newly rotated shape and explain its name with a boundary feature.
explanation: An adult draws and names a circle, triangle, square, rectangle, and hexagon. Trace each boundary. A circle has a curved boundary with no corners; triangles have three straight sides; hexagons have six. Count straight sides and corners carefully, marking a starting place so the first side is not counted twice.

A square has four equal straight sides and four square corners. A rectangle has four straight sides and four square corners; its sides need not all be equal. A square is therefore a special rectangle, although children may also use the more specific name square. The adult can show a square corner using the corner of paper.

Turn a shape drawing or make it larger: its defining features stay. A triangle pointing sideways is still a triangle, and a square balanced on a corner is still a square. Color, position, and size are useful descriptions but do not decide the shape name. Curved or open three-line drawings are not triangles.

examples.prompt: An adult draws a closed shape with 3 straight sides, pointing to the left. Name it.
steps: Trace the closed boundary.
Count three straight sides and three corners.
Its direction does not change those features, so it is a triangle.

examples.prompt: Turn a paper square so one corner points up. Did it stop being a square?
examples.answer: No, it is still a square.
steps: Before turning, trace four equal sides and four square corners.
Rotate the paper without bending or cutting it.
The same sides and corners remain, so its name stays square.

worksheets.title: Build and point: Flat shapes keep their names
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: An adult draws a circle, using a round cup rim as a guide. Trace it and name the flat shape.
steps: Trace the curved boundary.
There are no straight sides or corners.

items.prompt: Draw a closed shape using exactly 3 straight sides. Name it.
steps: Join three straight sides end to end.
Close the boundary to form three corners.

items.prompt: An adult draws a wide rectangle with four square corners. Count its sides.
steps: Start at one side and trace around.
Count each of the four straight edges once.

items.prompt: An adult draws a closed 6-sided shape with straight sides. Name it.
steps: Trace each straight side once.
Six sides identify a hexagon.

items.prompt: Compare an adult-drawn small circle and large circle. Do they have the same shape name?
steps: Both have round curved boundaries and no corners.
Changing size does not change those features.

items.prompt: An adult draws a triangle with its point down. Is triangle still a correct name?
steps: Count its three straight sides.
Direction does not change the side count.

worksheets.title: Draw and explain: Flat shapes keep their names
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: An adult draws 3 straight segments that do not join into a closed boundary. Is the drawing a triangle?
steps: A triangle must be closed.
The open ends prevent a three-sided closed shape.

items.prompt: Name a flat shape with 4 equal sides and 4 square corners.
items.answer: Square; it is also a rectangle.
steps: Check that all four side lengths match.
The four square corners make it a special rectangle.

items.prompt: An adult draws a red triangle and a blue triangle of different sizes. What feature gives both their name?
items.answer: Both are closed shapes with 3 straight sides.
steps: Ignore the colors and sizes.
Trace three joined straight sides on each.

items.prompt: A puppet calls every four-sided shape a square. Explain one missing check.
items.answer: Check for four equal sides and four square corners.
steps: Four sides alone are not enough.
A long rectangle has four sides without all being equal.

items.prompt: An adult draws a square and a circle. Which has corners, and how many?
items.answer: The square has 4 corners; the circle has none.
steps: Trace where the square's straight sides meet.
The circle's boundary stays curved with no corners.

items.prompt: Trace a hexagon drawn by an adult. Mark one starting corner and count all corners.
steps: Follow the six joined sides around the boundary.
Stop at the marked start without counting it twice.

worksheets.title: Use and check: Flat shapes keep their names
worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: Design a pretend flag using one triangle and one circle. Point to each and explain its name.
items.answer: A triangle with three straight sides and a circle with no corners.
steps: Draw the two closed boundaries.
Use sides and corners to identify each, not its color.

items.prompt: A sign is a square tilted to stand on a corner. An adult calls it a diamond. What mathematical shape name still fits?
steps: Tilting preserves four equal sides.
The same four square corners remain.

items.prompt: An adult draws a long rectangle, then turns the paper. Describe what stays the same.
items.answer: It remains a rectangle with 4 sides and 4 square corners.
steps: Turning moves the drawing as a whole.
No boundary feature changes.

items.prompt: An adult draws a hexagon and a triangle. Trace their sides. How are these shapes alike and different?
items.answer: Both have straight sides and corners; the hexagon has 6 sides and the triangle has 3.
steps: Trace both closed boundaries and notice the straight segments.
Count six sides on the hexagon and three on the triangle.

items.prompt: Make a triangle with one long side and two shorter sides that meet to close it. Is it allowed to have unequal sides?
steps: The defining check is three straight joined sides.
Triangles do not need all sides equal.

items.prompt: Describe a shape for an adult to draw without saying its name: choose circle or triangle.
items.answer: For example, draw a closed curve with no corners for circle, or a closed shape with 3 straight sides for triangle.
steps: Name the boundary features.
Check the adult's drawing against those features.

weeks.title: Flat pictures and solid objects
weeks.objective: Distinguish flat shapes from solids and identify sphere, cube, cone, and cylinder models.

connection.before: Identify circles, triangles, squares, rectangles, and hexagons by features across size and orientation.
connection.after: Count and compare collections of named flat shapes and solids through 10.

days: Contrast a circle drawing with a ball and name flat versus solid.
Explore or gesture through the described solids in sheet A.
Use sheet B to connect surface features with flat shapes and movement.
Plan pretend structures and give mystery clues with sheet C.
Identify a solid in a new orientation and explain one defining feature.
explanation: A flat shape is described on a surface: a circle drawing has length and width but is not a ball. A solid extends in three directions. Use ordinary examples with adult help: a ball models a sphere, a can models a cylinder, a cube-shaped block models a cube, and a party-hat form models a cone.

Compare the parts of solids. A cube has six flat square faces. A cylinder has two flat circular ends and a curved surface between them. A cone has a flat circular base and a curved surface narrowing to one point. A sphere has a curved surface all around with no flat face.

Real objects are models and may have seams or small extra parts. Attend to the overall mathematical form described in each task. Rolling or stacking gives evidence but does not alone name a solid: cylinders can roll on their side and stand on an end. Changing orientation does not change the solid.

examples.prompt: Compare a circle drawn on paper with a round ball. Which models a flat shape and which a solid?
examples.answer: The circle is flat; the ball models a sphere, a solid.
steps: Trace the circle on the paper surface.
Notice that the ball extends out in all directions and can be held.
Name the flat outline circle and the solid form sphere.

examples.prompt: A solid has two flat circular ends joined by one curved surface. Name it.
steps: Find the two circular ends described.
Notice the curved surface joining them.
Together those features identify a cylinder, even if it lies on its side.

The block extends in three directions.

A sphere has no flat face.

items.prompt: Which solid has square faces: cube or cylinder?

A cylinder's flat ends are circles.

items.prompt: An adult rolls a cylinder on its side, then stands it on an end. Explain why it can do both.

steps: The curved side supports rolling.
A flat end supports standing.

steps: The cylinder end is circular.
Tracing that boundary makes the same flat shape as the drawing.
items.skill: Connecting a face to a flat shape

items.answer: Flat: rectangle, hexagon. Solid: sphere, cube.
steps: Rectangles and hexagons are flat boundary shapes.
Spheres and cubes are three-dimensional solids.

items.prompt: For a pretend tower, choose between an ideal sphere and a cube for a flat base. Explain your choice.
items.answer: Cube, because it has flat square faces.
steps: A flat face rests evenly on a flat surface.
A sphere has a curved surface and can roll.

items.prompt: A toy is described as having no corners and no flat faces. Which fits: cube, sphere, or cone?
steps: A cube has corners and flat faces.
A cone has a point and flat base, leaving sphere.

items.prompt: An adult shows or describes a cube turned onto a different face. Are its faces still square?
steps: Turning leaves each face unchanged.
All six faces remain squares.

items.prompt: Draw a flat circle and tell an adult a different name for its round solid partner.
steps: The drawing is flat and named circle.
A round solid with curved surface all around is a sphere.

items.prompt: Which ideal solid could leave a circular outline if its flat end were traced: cylinder or cube?
steps: The cylinder has circular flat ends.
The cube's flat faces would trace squares.

items.prompt: Describe a mystery solid with enough information for an adult to identify cube, cone, sphere, or cylinder.
items.answer: For example, six square faces identifies cube; another accurate defining description is valid.
steps: Choose a solid and state its surface or face features.
Check that the clues distinguish it from the other three.

weeks.title: Compare shape collections

connection.before: Distinguish flat shapes from solids and identify sphere, cube, cone, and cylinder models.
connection.after: Choose matching or counting to justify comparisons through 10 and identify shapes independently.

days: Identify the whole object being counted in a shape picture.
Use sheet A to pair shape collections and record numerals.
Discuss side-count versus object-count errors on sheet B.
Apply comparisons to sign and design tasks on sheet C.
Describe one shape property and separately justify a comparison between two collections.
explanation: An adult can draw flat shapes and use written labels read aloud for solids. Count one whole shape or object at a time; do not count a triangle as three objects because it has three sides. First identify what collection the question names, then count only those members.

Compare shape collections with the matching methods already learned. A row of large triangles may have fewer objects than a row of tiny circles. Use number labels as a second representation after counting. Shape features decide the name, while one-to-one matching decides which collection has more.

Discuss two properties separately. A group can contain more circles than squares while squares have more corners per shape. Keep the question clear: are we comparing how many objects, or describing one object? This distinction helps children explain their evidence without mixing side counts and object counts.

examples.prompt: A drawing has 2 triangles and 5 circles. Which kind appears more often?
steps: Count whole shapes: two triangles and five circles.
Pair two triangles with two circles.
Three circles remain, so circles appear more often.

examples.prompt: There are 3 cube models and 3 sphere models. A child says cubes are more because they have corners. Compare object counts.
steps: Count each whole cube once, not each corner.
Count each sphere once.
Three pairs match, so corners do not affect the object counts.

steps: Count each closed shape once.
Four pairs leave two triangles.

items.prompt: Pretend 2 counters are cubes and 5 are spheres, kept in named groups. Which group has fewer solids?
steps: Two cube counters pair with two sphere counters.
Three sphere counters remain.

items.prompt: Draw 3 small circles and 3 large circles. Compare their numbers.
steps: Give each small circle one large-circle partner.
Both groups run out together.

items.prompt: An adult describes 1 hexagon and 4 rectangles. Which kind has more objects, regardless of sides?
steps: There is only one whole hexagon.
Four whole rectangles outnumber one hexagon.
items.skill: Separating side count from object count

items.prompt: Model a shelf with 7 cylinders and 6 cones using two counter groups. Choose the greater number label.
steps: Count both labeled groups.
Seven exceeds six by one unmatched object.

items.prompt: An adult draws 5 triangles, some pointing up and some down. Does direction split them into different shape names?
steps: Each closed shape still has three straight sides.
Turning does not change membership in the triangle group.

worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. items.prompt: A puppet counts the corners of 2 triangles and says there are 6 triangles. Correct the object count.
steps: Six counts the corners across both shapes.
Count each whole triangle once to get two.

items.prompt: In an adult-read display there are 8 circles and 8 squares. Compare counts, then name which shape has corners.
steps: Eight pairs show equal numbers of shapes.
A square has four corners; a circle has none.

items.prompt: An adult draws 6 rectangles and 4 circles. A child points to circles as the larger collection because they take more space. Check.
steps: Count six rectangles and four circles.
Four pairs leave two rectangles regardless of drawing size.

items.prompt: Name the two solid groups in this list, then compare their counts: 4 spheres, 2 cubes, 3 triangle drawings.
items.answer: Spheres and cubes are solid types; spheres are more numerous than cubes.
steps: A triangle drawing is flat, so set it aside for the solid comparison.
Four spheres outnumber two cubes.

items.prompt: Draw more triangles than circles using 5 shapes total, with at least one of each.
items.answer: For example, 3 triangles and 2 circles; 4 and 1 also works.
steps: Choose positive group counts that total five.
Pair them to confirm that triangles have leftovers.

items.prompt: An adult reads two labels: 9 hexagons and 7 squares. Which group has fewer shapes?
steps: Nine and seven are counts of whole shapes.
Seven is less than nine.

items.prompt: A pretend sign maker has 3 circle signs and 5 triangle signs. Which kind could cover more posts, one sign per post?
steps: Each whole sign covers one post.
Five triangle signs cover more posts than three circle signs.

items.prompt: Make two equal shape collections using 8 counters total, one named cubes and one named cylinders.
steps: Share one counter to each group repeatedly.
Four complete pairs use all eight.

items.prompt: A drawing shows 2 large squares and 7 tiny triangles. Explain why object size cannot decide which group has more.
steps: Count one whole shape per count word.
Tiny shapes still each count as one.

items.prompt: An adult describes 4 cones standing upright and 4 cones lying sideways. Are the group counts and shape names alike?
steps: Both descriptions name the same solid form.
Four objects in each group make equal quantities.

items.prompt: Design a shape picture with 6 circles and fewer squares, but at least 1 square. Tell both counts.
steps: Count six circles and the chosen square amount.
Matching leaves circles without square partners.

items.prompt: Give an adult a comparison clue for 5 cubes and 3 spheres without using the word more.
items.answer: For example, after making three pairs, two cubes have no sphere partners.
steps: Match three cubes to the three spheres.
Describe the two leftover cubes as evidence.

weeks.title: Explain a fair comparison
weeks.objective: Choose matching or counting to justify comparisons through 10 and identify shapes independently.

connection.before: Count and compare collections of named flat shapes and solids through 10.
connection.after: Act out and draw joining stories within 10, connecting both parts to a total.

days: Review when to use shape features and when to use object counts.
Select comparison methods and identify forms on sheet A.
Check incorrect labels and naming claims using sheet B.
Use picnic, riddle, and creation tasks from sheet C as oral demonstrations.
Explain one new numeral comparison and one new shape identification without a model.
explanation: This workshop joins two kinds of evidence. To compare quantities, count or pair whole objects. To name a shape, inspect sides, corners, faces, and curved surfaces. Ask the child to select the evidence that answers the actual question instead of applying one rule to every task.

When two reports disagree, rebuild the collections described. Pair each object only once and recount if necessary. Say which collection is greater, which is smaller, or why both are equal. A useful explanation can be a demonstration with counters while the adult records the words.

Continue short oral counts from numbers within thirty with adult support. Counting forward gives number order, but the child still needs to connect numeral labels to amounts. Avoid speed pressure; the goal is an accurate independent choice of method and a clear reason.

examples.prompt: Two pretend trays hold 7 round tokens and 9 square tokens. The round tokens are larger. Which tray has more tokens?
steps: Count whole tokens: seven round and nine square.
Make seven pairs, leaving two square tokens.
Those leftovers prove more square tokens, regardless of physical size.

examples.prompt: A mystery shape is flat, closed, has 4 equal straight sides, and has 4 square corners. Name it after turning it sideways.
steps: Use flat to rule out solids.
The four equal sides and four square corners identify a square.
Turning preserves those features, so the name remains square.

worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials. Accept pointing, moving, drawing, or an oral explanation; write dictated answers. Read numerals aloud if needed. Choose a few tasks at a time; these sheets are alternatives, not a one-sitting quota.

items.prompt: An adult reads 10 and 6. Choose a counting or matching method and explain which is greater.
steps: Build both counts or name their positions in the sequence.
Six pairs leave four objects in the ten group.

items.prompt: Compare 4 large circle drawings with 4 small triangle drawings by number of objects.
steps: Match one whole circle to one whole triangle.
Four pairs use both sets completely.

items.prompt: A solid with two flat circular ends is standing upright. Name it and tell whether it is flat or solid.
steps: The two circular ends with curved connecting surface identify a cylinder.
It extends in three directions.

items.prompt: Continue the adult-read count from 24 through 28.
steps: Start at the given twenty-four.
Advance one number word at a time to twenty-eight.

items.prompt: An adult draws a closed shape with 3 straight sides of different lengths. Name it.
steps: Count its three straight boundary segments.
Equal side lengths are not required.

items.prompt: Make a group of 5 and a group smaller than 5 but not empty. State the comparison.
items.answer: 5 is greater than any chosen 1, 2, 3, or 4.
steps: Count the chosen second group.
Pairing leaves counters in the five group.

worksheets.directions: Adult: read each task aloud and prepare any described drawing or paper pieces. Use ordinary counters (buttons, blocks, or paper circles), paper, and a pencil unless the task names other household materials.
