connection.before: Draw or build flat shapes and solid models, explaining sides, corners, faces, and position.
connection.after: Use positional language, shape composition, and counts to communicate an original small design.

days: Prepare the specified square and diagonal triangle pieces with adult help.
Join pieces and trace outer boundaries using sheet A.
Compare layouts and inspect internal shared edges on sheet B.
Build windows, paths, and original pictures with sheet C.
Compose a larger shape and explain how pieces touch and which boundary gives its name.
explanation: Place shapes together so their edges touch without gaps or overlaps. The large shape is described by its outside boundary. A shared edge inside the combined figure separates pieces, but it is not part of the outer boundary. Trace only the outside when naming the combined shape.

An adult can prepare two equal paper squares and one square cut along a corner-to-opposite-corner diagonal into two matching triangles. Put the triangle pieces back along their cut edges to rebuild the original square. Side-by-side equal squares form a rectangle when one full edge of each is shared.

Arrangement matters. The same pieces can make different outlines if they meet on different edges or only at a corner. Ask the child to describe how pieces touch, not merely how many pieces were used. Building, tracing, and turning the completed figure all give evidence about its shape.

examples.prompt: Two equal squares are placed side by side with one complete edge shared and outer sides aligned. Name the combined outside shape.
steps: Join the squares along a full equal-length edge with no gap.
Trace the outside, ignoring the shared inside edge.
The outline has four straight sides and four square corners, with two longer sides, so it is a rectangle.

examples.prompt: An adult cuts a square diagonally from one corner to the opposite corner. Put the two triangle pieces back along the cut. What whole returns?
steps: Identify the two matching triangle pieces.
Match their diagonal cut edges without gaps or overlap.
The outside returns to four equal sides and four square corners, making the square.

items.prompt: An adult draws two equal squares sharing a full side. Count the small pieces, then trace and count the outside corners. Are those counts the same?
items.answer: 2 pieces and 4 outside corners; the counts differ.
steps: Each square is one piece, giving two pieces.
Tracing the combined outside gives four corners; pieces and corners are different counting units.

items.prompt: An adult cuts a paper square along a diagonal. Count and name the pieces before rejoining them.
steps: A corner-to-opposite-corner cut divides the square in two.
Each piece has three straight sides.

items.prompt: Place the two triangle pieces from a diagonally cut square back together. Point to the edge that becomes hidden inside the whole.
steps: The pieces meet along those cut edges.
That shared edge is internal rather than part of the outside square.

items.prompt: Put 3 equal squares in one straight row, each sharing full sides with its neighbors. Name the outer shape.
steps: Aligned squares create straight top and bottom edges.
The outside has four square corners and two long sides.

items.prompt: An adult places 2 equal squares with only one corner touching. Does this arrangement make the same rectangle as full-edge joining?
steps: Corner contact leaves a different outline and unfilled spaces.
A rectangle from two squares requires a shared full edge.

items.prompt: Draw a square with one diagonal line. Does the inside line change the outside boundary's shape?
steps: The diagonal is inside the original boundary.
The four equal outside sides and square corners remain.

items.prompt: A puppet counts the shared line between two joined squares as an outside side. Explain the correction.
items.answer: Do not count the inside shared line when tracing the outer boundary.
steps: The line has square material on both sides.
Only edges bordering the exterior belong to the outline.

items.prompt: Arrange 4 equal square paper pieces as 2 rows of 2, all edges aligned with no gaps. Name the large outline.
steps: Each outer side spans two equal small-square edges.
All four outer sides are equal and corners are square.

items.prompt: The same 4 equal squares are arranged in one straight row. Name the new outline.
steps: The row is four small squares long and one high.
It has four square corners but not four equal side lengths.

items.prompt: Compare the 2-by-2 and one-row arrangements of 4 equal squares. What stays the same about the pieces?
items.answer: The same 4 square pieces are used.
steps: No piece is added or removed.
Only the placement and outer shape change.

items.prompt: Two triangle pieces from a diagonally cut square overlap when placed back. Does that exactly rebuild the square? Explain.
items.answer: No; they must meet along the cut edges without overlap or gaps.
steps: Overlap covers one region twice.
Matching the cut edges restores the original whole correctly.

explanation: A neighborhood drawing can use circles for ponds, squares for buildings, triangles for roofs, and rectangles for paths. These are flat picture parts, even when they stand for solid real objects. Name the shape you actually drew and explain what it represents.

explanation: A story picture should show the known amounts and the action. For arrivals, draw the starting group and the group moving in. For departures, mark the objects leaving so they are not counted as remaining. For hidden parts, show the stated whole and visible amount through a counter model even if the picture covers some objects.

Tell the question explicitly. How many arrived, how many altogether, and how many remained ask for different quantities. Have the child point to the part or whole named by the answer. An adult writes a matching equation only after the child explains the picture, so symbols record the reasoning.

Check a partner or puppet picture against every story detail. A correct final number can still accompany the wrong action. Retell using the model, count or recognize small facts, and rebuild the whole when checking a separation. Use totals at most ten, with fluent facts within five as familiar anchors.

Correct mismatched teen and oral records with sheet B.
Apply ten reasoning to fresh tray and seat contexts on sheet C.
Present a new number model and continue both a ones segment and a tens segment.
explanation: A collection can be checked at two levels: count every individual object, then organize a group of ten and any extras. The two methods should agree. Teen numerals 11–19 record one ten-group and one through nine additional ones. Twenty can be shown as two full ten-frames and checked by counting all twenty.

A missing part to ten is different from an extra part beyond ten. For eight in a ten-frame, two more fill the frame. For ten and eight extra ones, the whole is eighteen. Ask what amount is already present and what whole the question names before choosing a count.

Oral counting can travel farther than the object collections used for written records. An adult may prompt at a difficult decade boundary, then the child resumes. Practise both ones and tens and check the sequence against the supplied segment. These are counting tasks, not operations with two-digit written numbers.

examples.prompt: A collection contains 17 counters. Show a count-by-ones check and a ten-part check.
